subject: The World Around Us
period_schedule_display:
Period schedule:
  Row 1: 40 minutes × 16 periods = 640 minutes
Total: 16 periods · 10h 40min

periods.textbook_anchor: Green School — Walk around the school and create its map, including main building, playground, garden, water tanks, gate, and pathways (p. 56)
materials: large blank paper or chart sheet

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the opening conversation between Aasha and Mohit from Textbook p. 56, pausing to ask: what makes a school feel like a good place? Students share briefly.
Class discusses what features their school has — buildings, garden, taps, pathways — and the teacher lists them on the board as a collective reference.

Following the prompt on Textbook p. 56, students walk around the school in pairs, observing and noting key features: main building, playground, garden, water tanks, gate, pathways. On return, each pair begins sketching a rough campus map.

Students complete their maps at their desks, labelling each feature clearly. Teacher circulates, prompting students to look for features they may have overlooked — water-related spots, trees, notice boards.
Quick share: two or three students hold up maps and name one feature they had not noticed before the walk.

periods.implied_lo: Students can observe a local institution's physical layout and represent it as a labelled map.
periods.section_context: School campus walk; main building, playground, garden, water tanks, school gate, pathways; campus map drawing.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which spot on your map do you think is the most useful for everyone, and why?' Pairs naturally surface different priorities — shade, water, safety — making the map a living document of student values rather than a copying exercise.

periods.activity_title: What I Love and How I Can Help
periods.textbook_anchor: Green School — Write what you really like about your school and how you can make it greener (p. 57)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the idea of a 'green school' — one that manages waste, saves water, uses electricity carefully, and has a green campus — drawing from Textbook p. 57. Brief class discussion: what would a green school look and feel like?
Each student writes individually in response to the prompts on Textbook p. 57: what they really like about their school, and how they could make it greener.

Students also write a short response to the safety prompt on Textbook p. 57: in case of any difficulty at school, whom would they talk to or inform? Teacher clarifies why identifying a trusted adult matters.
Pair-share: students exchange notebooks and read each other's 'green school' ideas, adding one suggestion in the margin with the partner's permission. Teacher listens in and notes interesting ideas.
Class closes with three volunteers sharing their most original green idea. Teacher affirms that caring for school is itself a form of civic responsibility.

periods.implied_lo: Students can articulate what they value about a shared institution and propose concrete improvements to make it more sustainable.
periods.section_context: Green school concept; waste management, water saving, electricity care, green campus; whom to inform in difficulty at school.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Prompt students to think locally: 'Which idea could your class actually try this week, with no extra cost?' This keeps the writing purposeful rather than aspirational and connects expression to action.

periods.textbook_anchor: Be a School Explorer! — Form explorer teams (Water Watchers, Electricity Savers, Waste Warriors, Green Guardians, Traffic Trackers) to observe and report on different aspects of the school environment (p. 58)
materials: observation prompt cards (teacher-prepared, one per team)

time_bands.activity: Teacher explains the School Explorer framework: five teams, each with a specific focus area — Water Watchers, Electricity Savers, Waste Warriors, Green Guardians, Traffic Trackers. Class is divided into five groups. Each group receives an observation prompt card listing what to look for.

Teams move through the school — or within the classroom and visible corridor — observing their assigned domain: leaking taps, lights or fans left on, litter, plants and trees, movement near the gate. Each student records what they see using words or quick sketches.
Teams reassemble in the classroom. Each group organises their observations into a brief report — what they found, what was working well, and what needs attention.
One spokesperson from each team shares a single key finding with the class. Teacher records these on the board, grouped by domain, as a shared class record.

periods.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured observation of a familiar environment, organise findings by category, and report them to a group.
periods.section_context: School Explorer Teams: Water Watchers, Electricity Savers, Waste Warriors, Green Guardians, Traffic Trackers; leaking taps, wasted electricity, litter, plants and trees, traffic near school gate; team observation and reporting.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask the Green Guardians: 'Did you notice any traditional or local ways the school or nearby area keeps things clean or cool?' This naturally opens the floor to practices like cow-dung floor cleaning without labelling them — students connect lived knowledge to the exploration.

periods.textbook_anchor: Waste Management — Make paper chits naming different waste items and sort them into three boxes: green for wet waste, blue for dry waste, and a third for items for the recycler (p. 61)
materials: small paper chits (prepared in class — blank slips)
three boxes or large envelopes labelled green, blue, and 'for recycler'
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing three labelled bins (green, blue, recycler)

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Waste Management section with the class, covering dry and wet waste categories, bin colour codes, and the role of traditional recyclers who collect specific materials in different regions. Students note the colour codes on the board.

Each group receives blank slips. Following Textbook p. 61, students write the names or draw items they know from school or home — food peels, paper, bottles, cloth scraps, broken pens — creating a set of chits. Groups add their own items beyond the textbook list.

Groups take turns picking chits one by one and placing each in the correct box — green, blue, or recycler. After all chits are placed, the group reviews one box at a time and debates any item they are unsure about, reaching a group decision.
Class discussion following Textbook p. 62: what happens if we do not separate our waste? Teacher draws out consequences for sanitation workers, the environment, and the community.
Students write the two bin colours and what goes in each in their notebooks — a quick personal reference.

periods.implied_lo: Students can classify everyday materials into waste categories by applying a rule-based sorting system.
periods.section_context: Dry waste and wet waste categories; green bin, blue bin, recycler box; food peels, paper, bottles, cloth scraps; traditional recyclers; consequences of not separating waste.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Does anyone know what the recycler in your area is called, and what they collect?' Different regions use different names and collect different materials — welcoming these answers honours community knowledge and makes the lesson locally real. Prompt the class to think about whether there are items that could be reused before they reach any bin.

periods.activity_title: Honouring Sanitation Workers — Discussion and Writing
periods.textbook_anchor: Waste Management — Discuss what we can do to make the work of sanitation workers easier and safer (p. 62)

time_bands.activity: Teacher poses the discussion prompt from Textbook p. 62: what is the work of sanitation workers, and what challenges might they face every day? Students share what they know from their neighbourhoods or school.

Small groups discuss two questions in parallel: what can students do to make sanitation workers' jobs easier, and what role does proper waste segregation play in their safety? Groups record two or three concrete actions.

Groups share their ideas with the class. Teacher guides the conversation toward dignity and respect — why it matters that every student segregates waste carefully, not just as an environmental act but as a social one.
Each student writes a short response in their notebook: two things they commit to doing so that their school's sanitation workers have a safer day. These are personal statements, not a class pledge.
Teacher closes by affirming that what we do with our waste is not just about the environment — it directly affects the people who manage it.

periods.implied_lo: Students can connect their own everyday behaviour to the conditions and dignity of workers who manage shared spaces.
periods.section_context: Sanitation workers' challenges; waste segregation as a social act; student actions to reduce unsafe waste handling; dignity and respect for community workers.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If a sanitation worker visited our class today, what is one thing you would want to tell them, and one thing you would want to ask?' This reframes students as respectful interlocutors rather than passive recipients of a lesson about others.

periods.activity_title: Black and White Tiles — Heat Absorption Inquiry
periods.textbook_anchor: Let Us be Cool! — Paint one tile or stone black and another white, place both under the Sun, and compare which feels cooler after a while (p. 62)
materials: access to sunlight (window ledge or outdoors)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing sunlight hitting dark and light surfaces with arrows for absorbed vs reflected heat

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the question: why do some rooms feel warmer than others? Class discusses school-specific observations — roof colour, window direction, trees nearby. Teacher introduces the idea that surface colour affects heat absorption.

Following Textbook p. 62, students in groups prepare two tiles or stones: one wrapped or painted black, one white. Both are placed on the window ledge or in a sunny spot to absorb heat for a sustained period.

While waiting, students discuss and note: what other design choices make a building stay cool — trees, ventilated windows, white roofs? Teacher introduces the IKS note naturally: in many villages, floors are cleaned with cow dung and mud to keep insects away and maintain coolness.
Students carefully touch each tile and record their observation: which felt warmer, which felt cooler. Groups record findings in notebooks and write their conclusion about colour and heat.
Class shares findings. Teacher connects to the writing prompt on Textbook p. 63: what would happen if the school roof were painted white?
Students write a one-sentence prediction in their notebooks about the white roof, to be revisited in discussion.

periods.implied_lo: Students can test a hypothesis about the physical properties of everyday materials by designing and carrying out a simple comparative investigation.
periods.section_context: Black and white tiles or stones; heat absorption and reflection; surface colour and temperature; white roofs, ventilated windows, trees as cooling strategies; cow dung and mud floors as traditional cooling practice.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Before we tested, which colour did you think would be cooler, and why?' Surfacing prior hypotheses and then comparing them to results is the heart of inquiry — welcome wrong predictions as productive moments.

periods.activity_title: Keeping Cool — Discussion and Action Planning
periods.textbook_anchor: Let Us be Cool! — If your area is getting warmer, what actions can be taken to keep it cool? (p. 63)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with the prompt from Textbook p. 63: if your area is getting warmer, what actions can be taken to keep it cool? Students brainstorm individually for two minutes, then share ideas with a partner.

Whole-class discussion organised around two scales: what can an individual student or family do, and what would require the school or community to act together? Teacher records responses under both headings on the board.

Students evaluate the ideas on the board: which are already happening at school, which would be easy to start, and which would need more planning? Teacher guides the discussion to connect natural cooling strategies — trees, light-coloured surfaces, ventilation — to the concept of systems rather than single fixes.
Students write a short 'cooling action plan' for their classroom or school — listing three specific, doable changes. They write in first person to reinforce agency.
Teacher invites one or two students to read their plans aloud. Class affirms what is realistic and ambitious at the same time.

periods.implied_lo: Students can evaluate strategies for managing a natural phenomenon at different scales — individual, classroom, and community — and propose evidence-based actions.
periods.section_context: Warming of local areas; individual and community cooling strategies; trees, white surfaces, ventilation; connecting natural thermal management to school design.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which idea on our board came from something you have seen at home or in your neighbourhood?' Connecting community practice to scientific reasoning builds confidence that local knowledge is valid — not a lesser form of understanding.

periods.activity_title: Measuring a Drip — Quantifying Water Waste
periods.textbook_anchor: Dripping Water — Look for a dripping tap or make a small hole in a water bottle, collect the dripping water in a glass, measure how long it takes to fill, and calculate how many glasses would fill in a day (p. 64)
materials: sharp pin or needle to make a small hole

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the section: a single dripping tap wastes far more water than it seems. Class estimates: how many glasses of water do you think one dripping tap wastes in a full day? Students record their estimates before any measurement.
Following Textbook p. 64, each group sets up a used water bottle with a small pinhole, holds it over a glass, and times how long it takes for the glass to fill. Students record the time carefully.

Using their measured fill time, groups calculate how many glasses would fill in one hour, and then in one full day. Students write the calculation in their notebooks and compare their estimates with the actual result.

Groups share their calculations. Teacher leads a brief discussion: what would this amount look like if added up across all the taps in the school? How does this connect to the Jal Shakti Abhiyan and the idea that small actions have large effects?

Students note the discussion prompts from Textbook p. 64 in their notebooks: what can we do to prevent water wastage at school, and how can we collect and use rainwater? Brief sharing of two or three ideas to close.

periods.implied_lo: Students can collect and use simple measurement data to estimate the cumulative impact of a small, continuous process.
periods.section_context: Dripping tap; pinhole bottle; glass fill time; water wasted per hour and per day calculation; Jal Shakti Abhiyan; rainwater collection.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'At home, do you know of any traditional way water is stored or cooled without electricity?' The clay pot (matka) often comes up naturally here — welcome it as an example of smart, community-developed technology that manages water and keeps it cool through evaporation.

periods.activity_title: Water Conservation Commitments — Discussion and Writing
periods.textbook_anchor: Dripping Water — Discuss what easy things we can do in our school to prevent water wastage (p. 64)

time_bands.activity: Teacher opens with a reflection question: after measuring how much a single drip wastes, how does that change the way you think about a running tap? Students share reactions briefly before moving to structured discussion.

Class discusses the prompt from Textbook p. 64 in small groups: what easy things can we do in our school to prevent water wastage? Groups list specific, visible actions — turning off taps, reporting leaks, reusing water from bottles.

Groups share their lists. Teacher records on the board, grouping actions by who can do them: individual students, class as a group, or school administration. This surfaces the idea that conservation is both personal habit and collective system.

Each student writes a personal water commitment: one specific behaviour they will change and one they will encourage in a classmate. Teacher stresses that the commitment is honest and small — not a grand promise.
Two or three volunteers read their commitments aloud. Teacher affirms that daily small actions, taken together, are exactly how conservation campaigns like Jal Shakti Abhiyan work.

periods.implied_lo: Students can translate quantitative evidence about resource use into personal and collective conservation commitments.
periods.section_context: Water wastage; school-based conservation actions; individual habits and collective systems; Jal Shakti Abhiyan; personal water commitment.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which action on our list would be easiest to start tomorrow, and which would need someone else's help?' Distinguishing individual from systemic action is a key civic thinking habit — encourage students to name who else would need to be involved.

periods.textbook_anchor: Greenery Around Us — Take two glasses of water, measure their temperature, place one under a tree and one under the Sun, and after an hour compare the temperatures again (p. 66)
materials: access to a tree on campus and a sunny spot

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Greenery Around Us section introduction with the class, establishing that trees provide shade, clean air, food, and habitat. Students are asked: can a tree actually change the temperature of water nearby? They record their prediction.

Following Textbook p. 66, each group fills two identical glasses with water, measures the starting temperature of each using the thermometer, and records both readings. Both glasses go to their assigned spots — one under a tree, one in direct sunlight.

While the glasses sit, students complete the observation and naming tasks from Textbook p. 65: listing the trees on their campus or near their school, and recording birds and insects they have seen near those plants and trees. This is done from memory or by a quick look out the window.
Groups retrieve both glasses and measure the temperature again. They record the final readings and write a conclusion: what do these readings tell us about the role of trees in keeping spaces cool?
Two groups share their data and conclusions. Teacher connects the finding to planning a butterfly garden — one more way trees and plants make a school a habitat, not just a building.

periods.implied_lo: Students can use measured temperature data to draw a conclusion about the cooling effect of natural shade.
periods.section_context: Two glasses of water; thermometer readings before and after; tree shade versus direct sunlight; trees as providers of shade, clean air, food and habitat; campus trees; birds and insects on campus; butterfly garden planning.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which tree on your campus would you most want to sit under on a hot day, and why?' Students often know individual trees by character — location, spread, fruit — and this grounds the data in lived observation rather than abstraction.

periods.activity_title: Traffic Rules and Safety Signboard Design
periods.textbook_anchor: Traffic Signs — Find out and write at least three traffic rules, and observe and write about what you saw at the school gate (p. 67)
periods.visual_aids: Board listing two or three common traffic signs as reference

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the Traffic Signs section, reading Thomas's concern about road accidents near school from the textbook. Class discusses: what have you noticed near your school gate during arrival or dismissal? Brief sharing grounds the section in observation.

Following Textbook p. 67, students individually write at least three traffic rules they know or find out from each other, and then write a few sentences about what they observed or imagine happens at the school gate — movement, crowding, speed.

In teams, students design a safety signboard for the school gate using words, drawings, or symbols. The signboard must communicate a specific safety message clearly to drivers, parents, and students. Teams decide on the message, layout, and visual elements together.

Each team holds up their signboard. Class discusses: is the message clear from a distance? Would it actually change behaviour? Teacher invites the class to pick the most effective feature from each design.
Teacher poses the discussion prompt from Textbook p. 68: besides signboards, what else can students do to improve traffic safety near school? Two or three quick ideas are shared and noted.

periods.implied_lo: Students can apply knowledge of civic safety rules to design a clear, purposeful communication artefact for a public space.
periods.section_context: Traffic rules; school gate observations; safety signboard design using words, drawings, symbols; civic responsibility and student agency in public safety.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Who is your signboard's main audience — drivers, parents, or students — and how does that change what you draw or write?' Audience awareness makes the design task genuinely communicative rather than decorative.

periods.activity_title: Fire Drill Practice — Preparedness in Action
periods.textbook_anchor: Fire Safety — Write where the fire extinguisher is kept in your school and where the assembly point is; write what you should do if there is a fire or you smell smoke (p. 68–69)
periods.visual_aids: Board diagram showing the six fire drill steps

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads the Fire Safety section with the class, establishing why preparedness matters more than panic. Students identify: do they know where the school's fire extinguisher is? Where is the assembly point? Brief discussion reveals what students already know and do not know.

Following Textbook p. 68, students write the location of the fire extinguisher and the assembly point in their school. For students who do not know, a quick consult with the teacher or the board supplies the information — the writing task is a record, not a test of prior knowledge.

Teacher presents the six-step fire drill procedure on the board: move calmly to exits, crawl under smoke, avoid hiding places, help others safely, reach the assembly point, alert staff. Students write what they should do if they smell smoke, as prompted by Textbook p. 69, organising their response using the six steps.

Class practises a walk-through of the fire drill — not a full evacuation drill, but a calm, step-by-step rehearsal at their seats and then to the classroom door. Students narrate each step aloud as they practise it. Emphasis is on calm, orderly movement and helping a neighbour.
Quick reflection: what was the most important thing to remember? Two or three students share. Teacher affirms preparedness as a form of care for oneself and others.

periods.implied_lo: Students can recall and sequence the steps of an emergency response procedure and demonstrate calm, orderly behaviour during a practice.
periods.section_context: Fire extinguisher location; assembly point; six-step fire drill: move calmly, crawl under smoke, avoid hiding, help others safely, reach assembly point, alert staff; what to do if smelling smoke.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Why do we practise fire drills when there is no fire?' This surfaces the core idea that emergency preparedness is built through rehearsal — students connect the practice to the concept of being ready before a crisis arrives.

periods.activity_title: Situations That Matter — Group Discussion and Response
periods.textbook_anchor: What We do Matters! — In small groups, discuss the five situations of poor behaviour and decide what you would do and how to prevent such incidents (p. 70)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the section: the way we behave in shared spaces — school, home, public places — shapes whether those spaces feel welcoming or uncomfortable for everyone. Brief open question: have you ever felt uncomfortable because of how someone else behaved in a shared space?

Following Textbook p. 70, five groups each take one situation: queue-jumping at the water tap, bench vandalism with a silent bystander, littering copied by a younger student, teasing and mockery, and noise disturbing a public group. Each group discusses: if you see this happening, what would you do? What steps could prevent this from occurring?

One spokesperson from each group shares their group's response and prevention ideas with the class. Teacher facilitates cross-group connections: which situations involve bystanders? Which involve younger children copying older ones? How does that change what we can do?
Students write a short personal reflection: which situation felt hardest to respond to, and what made it hard? This is not shared — it is a private honest note to themselves.

periods.implied_lo: Students can analyse scenarios of social behaviour, identify the role of bystanders and community norms, and propose concrete responses.
periods.section_context: Queue-jumping at water tap; bench vandalism and silent bystander; littering copied by younger student; teasing and mockery; noise disturbing others in a public park; student responses and prevention strategies.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'In which situation would it be hardest to speak up, and why might that be?' This question surfaces social courage and peer pressure as real factors — honouring the difficulty rather than implying that the right action is always easy.

periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Draw a large happiness tree on chart paper; each student adds a leaf with one small action that makes school a happier place (p. 71)
materials: large chart paper or roll paper
green paper cut into leaf shapes (or students cut their own)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the reflection section: the chapter has covered waste, heat, water, greenery, safety, traffic, and social behaviour. Today the class brings all of it together through a shared creative act. Teacher reads the happiness tree prompt from Textbook p. 71 aloud.

A large tree outline is drawn on chart paper and fixed to a wall or board. Each student receives a leaf shape (or cuts one from green paper). Students individually write one small, specific action that makes school a happier place — one that they could actually do. Examples from the textbook: greeting someone, turning off lights, sharing space.

Students take turns adding their leaves to the tree, briefly reading their action aloud as they place it. Teacher encourages students who write something similar to notice the overlap — these are the highest-priority actions for the class.

Class looks at the completed tree together. Teacher facilitates a reading of the whole: which actions are about the environment, which are about behaviour with others, which are about safety? Students see the chapter's threads in their own words.
Each student writes the one action they are most committed to in their notebook — a personal anchor from the collective tree.

periods.implied_lo: Students can synthesise their learning about a shared institution by identifying and expressing specific, actionable contributions to its wellbeing.
periods.section_context: Happiness tree; leaf actions — greeting others, turning off lights, sharing space; environmental, behavioural, and safety actions; collective expression of school wellbeing.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which leaf on our tree would make the biggest difference for someone who often feels left out?' This question extends the tree from a celebration of action to a practice of perspective-taking and inclusion.

periods.activity_title: Diary from Another Perspective — Empathy Writing
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Write a diary entry from the perspective of a student who uses a wheelchair, a student who speaks a different mother tongue, or a sanitation worker at school (p. 71)

time_bands.activity: Teacher introduces the perspective-writing task from Textbook p. 71: today students write as someone else — someone whose experience of the same school is different from their own. The three options are introduced: a student who navigates school using a wheelchair, a student who speaks a different mother tongue, or a sanitation worker.

Brief whole-class discussion: what do you already know or imagine about any one of these three perspectives? Teacher draws out concrete details — the school corridor, the lunch break, the morning rush — to ground the writing in place rather than abstraction.

Students write their diary entry independently. Teacher circulates, prompting with specific questions: what did the day sound like for this person? What was easy? What made them smile or worry? Students write in first person, using 'I' as the chosen character.
Volunteers read their entries aloud. Class listens for one detail they had not thought of before. Teacher affirms specificity — a small, precise detail reveals more empathy than a broad statement.
Students write one sentence at the end of their diary entry: 'One thing I can do because of this perspective is ___.' This links empathy to action.

periods.implied_lo: Students can write from a perspective different from their own, identifying specific experiences of ease and difficulty within a familiar environment.
periods.section_context: Diary entry perspectives: student using a wheelchair, student with a different mother tongue, sanitation worker; feelings, ease, difficulty, and moments of happiness or worry in a school day.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'Which details in your diary entry are things you could actually change or help with, and which are bigger structural issues?' This distinction — between what one person can do and what requires collective change — is honest and important for Grade V students.

periods.activity_title: My Dream School — Survey, Speech, and Synthesis
periods.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Take a quick survey of five students and one teacher about what makes them happy, what could improve, and what kind act they saw; present findings to the class (p. 72)

time_bands.activity: Following Textbook p. 72, each student conducts a quick survey — asking five classmates and, where possible, one teacher — three questions: what makes them feel happy in school, what one thing could be improved, and what kind act they saw today. Students record responses in their notebooks.

Students compile their survey findings and identify one pattern: what came up most often? They prepare a two or three sentence oral summary of what they discovered. Teacher circulates and helps students notice connections between their findings and the chapter's themes — waste, water, heat, greenery, safety, behaviour.

Following Textbook p. 72, each student drafts a one-minute speech for morning assembly on 'My Dream School'. The speech must mention what makes the school special, who helps keep it that way, and what every student can do. Students draw on the full chapter's content — green practices, water conservation, thermal comfort, campus greenery, traffic safety, fire preparedness, and respectful behaviour — to build a vision grounded in evidence, not just aspiration.
Three or four volunteers deliver their speech to the class. Class listens for one specific, concrete idea they had not heard before. Brief appreciative sharing — what was strong about each speech?

Teacher closes the chapter: the school is a living system — natural and human-cultural at once. Every action students take as Water Watchers, Waste Warriors, Green Guardians, safe corridor walkers, and kind classmates contributes to a school that works well for everyone.

periods.implied_lo: Students can draw on evidence from across the chapter's environmental and civic themes to articulate a coherent, action-oriented vision of a well-functioning school.
periods.section_context: Peer and teacher survey: happiness, improvement, kind acts; one-minute speech on 'My Dream School'; chapter synthesis across green practices, water conservation, thermal comfort, campus greenery, traffic safety, fire preparedness, respectful behaviour.
periods.teacher_facilitation_note: Ask: 'If you could only keep one change from everything we explored in this chapter, what would it be and why?' This distillation question reveals which ideas have genuinely taken root — and listening to the range of answers shows students how many valid priorities exist within a single shared place.

coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students paint tiles black and white, expose both to sunlight, and compare which surface absorbs more heat.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can evaluate strategies for managing a natural phenomenon at different scales — individual, classroom, and community — and propose evidence-based actions.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Warming of local areas; individual and community cooling strategies; trees, white surfaces, ventilation; connecting natural thermal management to school design.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let Us be Cool! — If your area is getting warmer, what actions can be taken to keep it cool? (p. 63)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students discuss and write a cooling action plan identifying changes at individual and school-community scales.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can collect and use simple measurement data to estimate the cumulative impact of a small, continuous process.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Dripping tap; pinhole bottle; glass fill time; water wasted per hour and per day calculation; Jal Shakti Abhiyan; rainwater collection.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Dripping Water — Look for a dripping tap or make a small hole in a water bottle, collect the dripping water in a glass, measure how long it takes to fill, and calculate how many glasses would fill in a day (p. 64)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students time how long a pinhole bottle takes to fill a glass and calculate total water wasted per day.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can translate quantitative evidence about resource use into personal and collective conservation commitments.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Water wastage; school-based conservation actions; individual habits and collective systems; Jal Shakti Abhiyan; personal water commitment.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Dripping Water — Discuss what easy things we can do in our school to prevent water wastage (p. 64)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students discuss school-based water conservation actions and each write a specific personal conservation commitment.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can use measured temperature data to draw a conclusion about the cooling effect of natural shade.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Two glasses of water; thermometer readings before and after; tree shade versus direct sunlight; trees as providers of shade, clean air, food and habitat; campus trees; birds and insects on campus; butterfly garden planning.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Greenery Around Us — Take two glasses of water, measure their temperature, place one under a tree and one under the Sun, and after an hour compare the temperatures again (p. 66)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students measure and compare water temperature in tree shade versus direct sunlight to show trees' cooling effect.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can apply knowledge of civic safety rules to design a clear, purposeful communication artefact for a public space.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Traffic rules; school gate observations; safety signboard design using words, drawings, symbols; civic responsibility and student agency in public safety.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Traffic Signs — Find out and write at least three traffic rules, and observe and write about what you saw at the school gate (p. 67)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students write traffic rules, note school gate observations, and design a safety signboard for the school gate.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can recall and sequence the steps of an emergency response procedure and demonstrate calm, orderly behaviour during a practice.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Fire extinguisher location; assembly point; six-step fire drill: move calmly, crawl under smoke, avoid hiding, help others safely, reach assembly point, alert staff; what to do if smelling smoke.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Fire Safety — Write where the fire extinguisher is kept in your school and where the assembly point is; write what you should do if there is a fire or you smell smoke (p. 68–69)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students locate school emergency resources, write fire drill steps, and rehearse calm orderly evacuation movement.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can analyse scenarios of social behaviour, identify the role of bystanders and community norms, and propose concrete responses.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Queue-jumping at water tap; bench vandalism and silent bystander; littering copied by younger student; teasing and mockery; noise disturbing others in a public park; student responses and prevention strategies.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: What We do Matters! — In small groups, discuss the five situations of poor behaviour and decide what you would do and how to prevent such incidents (p. 70)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Five groups each analyse one social behaviour scenario and share response and prevention strategies with the class.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can synthesise their learning about a shared institution by identifying and expressing specific, actionable contributions to its wellbeing.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Happiness tree; leaf actions — greeting others, turning off lights, sharing space; environmental, behavioural, and safety actions; collective expression of school wellbeing.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Draw a large happiness tree on chart paper; each student adds a leaf with one small action that makes school a happier place (p. 71)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students add individual action leaves to a shared happiness tree, then identify their personal commitment.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can write from a perspective different from their own, identifying specific experiences of ease and difficulty within a familiar environment.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Diary entry perspectives: student using a wheelchair, student with a different mother tongue, sanitation worker; feelings, ease, difficulty, and moments of happiness or worry in a school day.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Write a diary entry from the perspective of a student who uses a wheelchair, a student who speaks a different mother tongue, or a sanitation worker at school (p. 71)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students write a first-person diary entry from the perspective of someone with a different school experience.

coverage_handoff.implied_lo: Students can draw on evidence from across the chapter's environmental and civic themes to articulate a coherent, action-oriented vision of a well-functioning school.
coverage_handoff.section_context: Peer and teacher survey: happiness, improvement, kind acts; one-minute speech on 'My Dream School'; chapter synthesis across green practices, water conservation, thermal comfort, campus greenery, traffic safety, fire preparedness, respectful behaviour.
coverage_handoff.textbook_anchor: Let us reflect — Take a quick survey of five students and one teacher about what makes them happy, what could improve, and what kind act they saw; present findings to the class (p. 72)
coverage_handoff.activity_summary: Students conduct a peer survey, find patterns, and draft and deliver a one-minute speech synthesising the chapter's themes into a vision for their school.

assessment_items.question_text: A student walks around her school to draw a map. Which feature is MOST important to include so that someone using the map can find water easily during a hot day?

options.label: A
options.text: The colours of the classroom doors

options.label: B
options.text: The location of water tanks and taps

options.label: C
options.text: The names of teachers in each room

options.label: D
options.text: The number of windows in the library

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The map task requires students to represent school features purposefully — water tanks and taps are both listed in the textbook activity and directly relevant to access during heat.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can observe a local institution's physical layout and represent it as a labelled map.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has not connected the map task to its functional purpose — noting decorative rather than useful features.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is confusing a physical-layout map with a directory of people — a different kind of institutional information.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is recording architectural details without evaluating which details serve the map's purpose for users.

assessment_items.question_text: A student wants to make her school greener. She has listed these ideas: planting a tree, turning off lights when leaving a room, and fixing a leaking tap. Choose ONE of these ideas and explain why it would make a real difference to the school environment.
expected_elements: Names one of the three listed ideas clearly.
Gives a specific reason why that action improves the school environment (e.g., a tree provides shade and habitat; turning off lights saves electricity; fixing a tap prevents water wastage).
Connects the action to something real in the school — not just a general statement.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any one of the three ideas if supported by a clear, specific reason. Vague responses such as 'it is good for nature' without explanation do not meet the expected elements.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can articulate what they value about a shared institution and propose concrete improvements to make it more sustainable.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

expected_elements: Names one of the three listed ideas clearly.
Gives a specific reason why that action improves the school environment (e.g., a tree provides shade and habitat; turning off lights saves electricity; fixing a tap prevents water wastage).
Connects the action to something real in the school — not just a general statement.

assessment_items.question_text: The Waste Warrior team walks through their school. They find: a used plastic bottle near the garden, lights on in an empty classroom, and a leaking tap near the drinking water area. Which of these findings belongs to the Waste Warrior team's report?

options.label: A
options.text: Both the lights and the leaking tap

options.label: B
options.text: The leaking tap near the drinking water area

options.label: C
options.text: The lights on in the empty classroom

options.label: D
options.text: The used plastic bottle near the garden

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The five explorer teams each have a specific domain — Waste Warriors focus on litter and solid waste, not electricity or water systems. This tests whether students understood the categorical structure of the inquiry.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can conduct a structured observation of a familiar environment, organise findings by category, and report them to a group.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has confused Waste Warriors with Electricity Savers — not retaining the domain boundaries of the explorer framework.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has confused Waste Warriors with Water Watchers — mixing two different environmental concerns.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student selected two findings from other domains, showing the domain categories were not consolidated.

assessment_items.question_text: Priya is sorting her school's waste. She has: a banana peel, an empty juice carton, and a crumpled newspaper. In which bins should each item go?

options.label: A
options.text: All three items → green bin because they all come from natural sources

options.label: B
options.text: Banana peel → blue bin; juice carton → green bin; newspaper → green bin

options.label: C
options.text: Banana peel → green bin; juice carton → blue bin; newspaper → blue bin

options.label: D
options.text: Banana peel → green bin; juice carton → green bin; newspaper → blue bin

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. Banana peel is wet waste (green bin); juice carton and newspaper are dry waste (blue bin). The item list is drawn directly from the chit activity in this section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can classify everyday materials into waste categories by applying a rule-based sorting system.

competency.competency_text: Identifies natural and humanmade systems that support their lives (water supply, water cycle, river flow systems, seasons, life cycle of plants and animals, food, household items, transport, communication, electricity in the home)

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has reversed the green and blue bin assignments — a direct colour-category confusion from the lesson.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is applying a misconception that 'natural origin' determines the wet-waste category, not understanding that processed/packaged items are dry waste regardless of source.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student correctly placed the banana peel but confused the juice carton's category — possibly associating liquids with the green bin.

assessment_items.question_text: Rajan's school does not separate waste. The sanitation workers have to sort through mixed garbage every day to find what can be recycled, often without gloves. Explain how students sorting waste correctly would make a real difference to the sanitation workers' daily experience. Use specific examples in your answer.
look_for: Identifies at least one specific risk or hardship sanitation workers face when waste is mixed (e.g., touching wet food waste while looking for dry recyclables, exposure to sharp objects hidden in garbage).
Explains how correct segregation removes or reduces that specific hardship.
Uses at least one concrete example of a waste item and which bin it belongs in.
Connects student behaviour to worker dignity, not just efficiency.
assessment_items.annotation: Strong responses will name a specific hazard and link it to a specific sorting action. Responses that stay at the level of 'it will be cleaner' without connecting to worker experience do not meet the ECR standard.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can connect their own everyday behaviour to the conditions and dignity of workers who manage shared spaces.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

look_for: Identifies at least one specific risk or hardship sanitation workers face when waste is mixed (e.g., touching wet food waste while looking for dry recyclables, exposure to sharp objects hidden in garbage).
Explains how correct segregation removes or reduces that specific hardship.
Uses at least one concrete example of a waste item and which bin it belongs in.
Connects student behaviour to worker dignity, not just efficiency.

assessment_items.question_text: Two tiles were placed in the Sun — one painted black and one painted white. After a while, the black tile felt much hotter. What does this tell us about which colour is better for painting a school roof, and why?
expected_elements: States that white is better for painting the school roof.
Explains that white surfaces reflect more sunlight and absorb less heat, keeping the building cooler.
Links the tile result directly to the roof choice — connects the experiment outcome to the real-world application.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept responses that correctly identify white and give a reason grounded in reflection versus absorption. A response that says 'white because it looks nice' does not meet the expected elements.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can test a hypothesis about the physical properties of everyday materials by designing and carrying out a simple comparative investigation.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: States that white is better for painting the school roof.
Explains that white surfaces reflect more sunlight and absorb less heat, keeping the building cooler.
Links the tile result directly to the roof choice — connects the experiment outcome to the real-world application.

assessment_items.question_text: A school in a hot region wants to keep its classrooms cooler. Which set of changes would be MOST effective, based on what you know about heat and cooling?

options.label: A
options.text: Keep windows closed, paint classrooms in dark colours, and run fans all day

options.label: B
options.text: Paint the roof black, close all windows, and remove trees near the building

options.label: C
options.text: Paint the roof white, plant trees near windows, and keep windows open for ventilation

options.label: D
options.text: Plant trees far from the building, paint walls grey, and add more electric lights

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. This item requires students to apply three connected cooling strategies from the section — colour, greenery, and ventilation — simultaneously. No single strategy alone is offered as a choice.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can evaluate strategies for managing a natural phenomenon at different scales — individual, classroom, and community — and propose evidence-based actions.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

what_each_option_reveals.B: The student has reversed the correct principles — selecting all three counterproductive strategies, indicating no consolidation of the heat-reflection and natural-cooling concepts.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student is thinking about comfort through mechanical means (fans) without applying the natural strategies, possibly not connecting surface colour and ventilation to thermal comfort.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student has partially engaged — trees appear but are placed incorrectly, and dark colours and artificial light show incomplete transfer of the cooling principles.

assessment_items.question_text: Anita's group found that a pinhole bottle filled one glass in 10 minutes. They calculated that the same drip would fill 144 glasses in one full day. What does this calculation tell us about the problem of dripping taps? Use the numbers in your answer.
expected_elements: References the specific numbers: one glass in 10 minutes and 144 glasses per day.
States that what seems like a tiny drip wastes a large amount of water when added up over time.
Connects the calculation to the need to fix leaking taps or take conservation action.
assessment_items.annotation: The numbers in the question are hypothetical but consistent with the type of calculation students performed. Accept any response that uses the numbers to argue scale of waste and connects to conservation. A response that only restates the numbers without interpretation does not meet the standard.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can collect and use simple measurement data to estimate the cumulative impact of a small, continuous process.

competency.competency_text: Performs simple inquiry related to specific questions independently or in groups

expected_elements: References the specific numbers: one glass in 10 minutes and 144 glasses per day.
States that what seems like a tiny drip wastes a large amount of water when added up over time.
Connects the calculation to the need to fix leaking taps or take conservation action.

assessment_items.task: You have just measured how much water a dripping tap wastes in one day. Now write two specific commitments — one thing you will do differently yourself, and one thing you will ask your class to do together — to reduce water waste in your school. Explain why you chose each one.
assessment_items.scaffold: My personal commitment: I will ___ because ___. My class commitment: We will ___ because ___.
format_of_output: Two written commitments, each with a 'because' explanation
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any specific, school-based commitment that is realistically doable. Vague commitments such as 'save water' without a specific action do not meet the standard. The personal and collective commitments may be different in scale.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can translate quantitative evidence about resource use into personal and collective conservation commitments.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student translates measurement evidence into concrete behavioural commitments at two levels — individual and collective — showing that conservation is both personal habit and social action.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold separates personal from collective commitment and requires a 'because' for each — preventing generic responses and ensuring the student links action to rationale.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: specific, school-based actions ('I will turn off the tap in the corridor after drinking' / 'We will check for leaking taps every Monday morning'). Weak: general statements ('save water', 'be careful') without specifying what, where, or how.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who find writing difficult may dictate their commitment to a partner who scribes. Students with strong ideas but limited writing fluency may use bullet points rather than full sentences — the quality of the commitment, not the prose, is assessed.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The scaffold's first-person format mirrors the personal-collective distinction built in the lesson and requires the student to own the commitment rather than describe it abstractly.

assessment_items.question_text: Two glasses of water were placed outside — one under a tree and one under the Sun. After an hour, the glass under the tree was 5°C cooler. What does this result tell us about the role of trees in a school campus? Give two reasons why schools should protect the trees on their grounds.
expected_elements: States that trees reduce temperature in the surrounding area by providing shade.
Gives a first specific reason trees should be protected (e.g., they keep the campus cooler, reducing heat stress for students and staff).
Gives a second distinct reason trees should be protected (e.g., they provide habitat for birds and insects, supporting biodiversity on the campus).
assessment_items.annotation: Award full marks for responses that name two genuinely distinct reasons. Responses that repeat the same reason in different words (e.g., 'cooler' and 'less hot') count as one. Accept any two reasons that appear in the Greenery Around Us section.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can use measured temperature data to draw a conclusion about the cooling effect of natural shade.

competency.competency_text: Demonstrates how natural resources can be shared, maintained, and conserved (trees, use of rainwater, benefits of millets)

expected_elements: States that trees reduce temperature in the surrounding area by providing shade.
Gives a first specific reason trees should be protected (e.g., they keep the campus cooler, reducing heat stress for students and staff).
Gives a second distinct reason trees should be protected (e.g., they provide habitat for birds and insects, supporting biodiversity on the campus).

assessment_items.task: Design a safety signboard for your school gate. Your signboard must communicate one clear safety message to drivers, parents, or students. Use words, drawings, or symbols — or a combination. Write one sentence below the signboard explaining who your main audience is and why you chose this message.
assessment_items.scaffold: My signboard message: [draw or write here]. My audience is ___ because ___.
format_of_output: A drawn or written signboard with a clear safety message
One explanatory sentence naming audience and reason for the message
assessment_items.annotation: Assess the clarity and appropriateness of the message for a public safety context, not artistic quality. A symbol-only signboard without the explanatory sentence is incomplete. Accept any safety message relevant to a school gate — slow down, no parking in front of gate, pedestrians first.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can apply knowledge of civic safety rules to design a clear, purposeful communication artefact for a public space.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student applies civic safety knowledge to a real design task, making choices about message, audience, and visual communication — moving from knowing rules to communicating them purposefully.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold separates the creative act (the signboard) from the reflective act (the audience sentence). Both are required. A student who draws without explaining the audience choice has completed only half the task.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: clear, readable message appropriate for the named audience; explanation names a specific group (e.g., 'drivers who are in a hurry') and gives a reason grounded in school gate observations. Weak: a generic 'be safe' message with no audience awareness.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who prefer not to draw may write the signboard text in large, clear letters. Students who draw without written words are accepted if the image clearly communicates one safety message. Teacher may ask the student to explain their symbol orally.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The signboard format mirrors the actual task in the Traffic Signs section and requires students to communicate for a real audience in a real public context, making the civic intent of the lesson concrete.

assessment_items.question_text: There is a fire alarm in school. Smoke is filling the corridor. Which action should a student take FIRST, according to the fire drill steps?

options.label: A
options.text: Hide under a desk until the smoke clears

options.label: B
options.text: Move calmly toward the nearest exit

options.label: C
options.text: Open all windows to let the smoke out

options.label: D
options.text: Run quickly to find the teacher

assessment_items.annotation: Correct answer is A. The six-step fire drill taught in this section begins with moving calmly to exits. The distractors each represent a specific wrong behaviour the section explicitly addresses.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can recall and sequence the steps of an emergency response procedure and demonstrate calm, orderly behaviour during a practice.

competency.competency_text: Discusses how to prepare for emergency situations (smoke, fire, small injuries, burns, electrical safety, unseasonal rains, fallen trees) based on discussions with family and community, or personal experiences

what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has retained the misconception that hiding is safe — the section explicitly states that hiding places should be avoided during a fire.
what_each_option_reveals.D: The student is prioritising finding adult help over self-evacuation — a common instinct, but the drill sequence establishes moving to the exit first before alerting staff.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student is confusing ventilation (useful in other situations) with fire safety protocol — opening windows can feed a fire and is not part of the drill steps.

assessment_items.question_text: In a school canteen queue, two older students push in front of younger ones. One younger student watches but does nothing. Another walks over and politely asks the older students to stand in line. What does the second student's action show about behaviour in shared spaces? Do you think it was the right thing to do? Give reasons for your answer.
look_for: Identifies that the second student's action demonstrates standing up for fairness and social norms in a shared space.

Evaluates whether the action was right, with at least one specific reason (e.g., everyone deserves equal access; polite correction models good behaviour for others; doing nothing allows the norm to persist).
Acknowledges the role of the bystander — why the first student's silence also has an effect.
Uses the concept that behaviour in shared spaces affects everyone, not just the individuals directly involved.
assessment_items.annotation: Accept responses that engage with the ethical dimension, not just the factual. A response that only says 'yes it was right because queue-jumping is wrong' without reasoning about shared spaces or bystander effect does not reach the ECR standard. Both sides of a reasoned disagreement are acceptable if supported.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can analyse scenarios of social behaviour, identify the role of bystanders and community norms, and propose concrete responses.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

look_for: Identifies that the second student's action demonstrates standing up for fairness and social norms in a shared space.

Evaluates whether the action was right, with at least one specific reason (e.g., everyone deserves equal access; polite correction models good behaviour for others; doing nothing allows the norm to persist).
Acknowledges the role of the bystander — why the first student's silence also has an effect.
Uses the concept that behaviour in shared spaces affects everyone, not just the individuals directly involved.

assessment_items.task: Think about all the things that make a school a happy, safe, and green place. Add your leaf to the class happiness tree: write one specific, small action that YOU can do to make your school better. Then write two sentences explaining how your action connects to either the environment, safety, or how people treat each other at school.
assessment_items.scaffold: My action leaf says: ___. This connects to [environment / safety / how we treat each other] because ___. If many students did this, it would ___.
format_of_output: One specific action written as a leaf message
Two explanatory sentences connecting the action to one of the three themes
Optional: a prediction of the collective effect
assessment_items.annotation: Accept any specific, doable action. Assess the explanatory sentences for whether they genuinely connect to a theme rather than just restating the action. 'Turn off the fan when leaving' connected to 'this saves electricity which is part of keeping our school green' is a strong response.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can synthesise their learning about a shared institution by identifying and expressing specific, actionable contributions to its wellbeing.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student identifies a specific contribution to school wellbeing and connects it to one of the chapter's three major themes — environment, safety, or social behaviour — showing synthesis across the chapter's content.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold's three-part structure (action, connection, collective effect) prevents students from stopping at the action alone. The third prompt is marked optional so that students who engage deeply are rewarded without penalising those who complete the core task.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: a specific action ('greet the sanitation worker each morning') with a clear connection ('this connects to how we treat each other because the sanitation worker deserves to feel respected'). Weak: 'be kind' with no connection to a specific theme.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students may draw their leaf action rather than write it. A student who draws and then explains verbally to the teacher may have the teacher scribe the explanation. All three themes are equally valid — no theme is more correct than another.
OPEN_TASK.format_type: Written or drawn leaf action with explanatory sentences
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The leaf format mirrors the collective happiness tree activity and preserves the sense that each student's contribution is part of a larger whole — making the individual act feel both personal and communal.

assessment_items.task: Write a diary entry for one day at school from the point of view of the school's sanitation worker. In your entry, describe: one moment in the day that was hard, one moment that made them feel respected or happy, and one thing a student did (or could do) that would make their work easier.
assessment_items.scaffold: Dear Diary, Today at school was ___. The hardest moment was when ___. I felt respected when ___. One thing a student could do to help me is ___.
format_of_output: A first-person diary entry in the voice of the sanitation worker
At least three moments covered: hard, respected/happy, and student action
assessment_items.annotation: Assess empathy depth and specificity — not prose quality. A response that names a concrete difficulty (e.g., sorting unsegregated waste, being ignored by students) and a concrete moment of respect (e.g., a student saying good morning, bins that are already sorted correctly) shows genuine perspective-taking. Generic responses ('it was a hard day') without specific school-based detail do not meet the standard.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can write from a perspective different from their own, identifying specific experiences of ease and difficulty within a familiar environment.

competency.competency_text: Learns about basic social and behavioural norms, values, and dispositions that benefit our social and natural environments and that help our society function smoothly (using dustbins, standing in queues, conserving water, using public transportation, keeping one's environment clean, always helping others in need regardless of background)

OPEN_TASK.what_this_demonstrates: The student inhabits another person's experience within a shared institution, identifying specific conditions of difficulty and respect — and connecting those conditions to their own daily choices about waste and behaviour.
OPEN_TASK.reading_the_scaffold: The scaffold names three distinct moments so students do not write a single-tone entry. Each moment is a different emotional register — difficulty, respect, actionable change — preventing a response that is uniformly negative or uniformly positive.
OPEN_TASK.strong_vs_weak_markers: Strong: names specific school locations, times of day, or student actions (e.g., 'at lunch the bins were full of mixed waste and I had to sort it by hand before I could clean the courtyard'). Weak: general statements that could describe any worker in any setting without school-specific detail.
OPEN_TASK.inclusivity: Students who prefer may write the entry about a student who uses a wheelchair or a student who speaks a different mother tongue — the assessment is about perspective-taking quality, not the specific perspective chosen. Students who find extended writing difficult may write in bullet points and read their entry aloud.
OPEN_TASK.format_rationale: The diary format creates an emotionally safe distance for students to explore empathy — writing as a character rather than about a character encourages deeper identification with the perspective and produces more specific, honest responses.

assessment_items.question_text: Imagine you are preparing a one-minute speech for your school's morning assembly on the topic 'My Dream School'. In your speech, you must mention: what makes a school a green, safe, and happy place; who helps keep it that way; and what every student can do. Write your speech below.
look_for: Mentions at least two specific environmental features of a green school (e.g., trees for shade, water conservation, waste segregation, white roofs).
Identifies at least one safety feature or practice (e.g., fire drill, traffic safety at the gate, knowing the assembly point).
Names specific people who contribute to keeping the school good (e.g., sanitation workers, teachers, students, traffic volunteers).
Includes at least one concrete action every student can take — not a general aspiration.
The speech holds together as a coherent whole, moving from what the school is to who maintains it to what students can do.
assessment_items.annotation: This is the synthesis item for the full chapter. Assess across all five look_for markers. A speech that covers only one section's content (e.g., only greenery) does not demonstrate chapter-wide synthesis. Strong responses will weave environmental, safety, and social themes into a single coherent vision. Award credit for specificity and coherence, not length.
assessment_items.implied_lo: Students can draw on evidence from across the chapter's environmental and civic themes to articulate a coherent, action-oriented vision of a well-functioning school.

competency.competency_text: Explains the functioning of local institutions (family, school, bank/post office, market, and panchayat) in different forms (story, drawing, tabulating data, reports), and analyses their roles
